latest_release.name: v2026.11.14: Experimental cache.sandbox for cached tasks
latest_release.body:
Cached tasks can now run in an experimental Linux sandbox. The sandbox blocks reads and writes that the task's cache declaration doesn't cover, so the task fails instead of storing a wrong result. `mise hook-env`, `mise env` and `mise ls` also run faster in projects with many tools.

## Added

- **`cache.sandbox` for cached tasks (experimental, enforced on Linux only).** A cached task is only correct if everything that affects its result is part of the cache key. With `cache.sandbox = true`, mise uses Landlock to restrict the task to its cache declaration. A read or write outside that declaration now makes the task fail instead of producing a cache entry that mise could restore for inputs it never checked. `cache.audit` only reports these reads after the run. [#16043](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/16043) (@jdx)

  ```toml
  [settings]
  experimental = true

  [tasks.build]
  run = "cat src/app.txt notes.txt > dist/out.txt"
  sources = ["src/**"]
  outputs = ["dist"]
  cache = { enabled = true, sandbox = true }
  ```

  In this example `notes.txt` is not listed in `sources`, so the task fails with `Permission denied`.

  - **Reads:** files matched by `sources`, the config files that define the task, outputs of its cached `depends` tasks, system paths and mise-installed tools. File names in the task directory can be listed, but other files' contents cannot be read.
  - **Writes:** only the directories that hold `outputs`, plus a private `TMPDIR` that all of the task's `run` entries share. The shared `/tmp` is blocked.
  - **Environment and network:** environment variables are limited to the essential ones, the task's own `env`, `cache.env`, `task_config.global_env` and `pass_through_env`. Network access is blocked.
  - **Extra paths:** add them with `allow_read` and `allow_write`. The paths become part of the cache key, but file contents do not, so a file that changes the result belongs in `sources`. Tools mise didn't install, such as a toolchain in `~/.cargo`, need an `allow_read` entry.
  - **Outputs:** outputs can't share a directory with sources. For example, `sources = ["*.c"]` with `outputs = ["*.o"]` is an error before the task starts. mise creates output directories before the run and removes any the task leaves empty.
  - **Configuration:** `task_config.cache` accepts the key, so you can turn it on for every eligible task. `--task-cache off` does not turn the sandbox off. `mise tasks ls --json` and `mise tasks info --json` show a `sandbox` field inside `cache`.
  - **Cache entries:** entries made in the sandbox are keyed separately, so mise never restores an entry stored without the sandbox for a task that asks for it.
  - **Other platforms:** on macOS and Windows, mise warns once and runs the task without the sandbox.

## Changed

- In file tasks, an invalid `#MISE cache=...` header is now an error. Previously mise warned and dropped the whole `cache` value. A `#MISE` header line with a key and no value, such as `#MISE deny_net=`, is also now an error. Previously mise skipped it silently, so the task ran without that restriction. [#16043](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/16043) (@jdx)

## Performance

- Every command does less redundant work. mise makes fewer filesystem checks, does much less memory copying, reads environment variables far less often and parses lockfile entries more cheaply. In a 29-tool project, `mise hook-env` makes about 13% fewer system calls. The environment-variable lookups per command drop from about 2,800 to about 500, which matters most in shells that export many variables. Behavior does not change. [#16044](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/16044), [#16050](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/16050), [#16051](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/16051), [#16052](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/16052) (@jdx)

## Documentation

- The security docs now include a [threat model](https://mise.jdx.dev/security.html#threat-model). It covers what mise trusts and where config trust, artifact verification a

Dev tools, env vars, and tasks in one CLI

Getting started • Docs • Dev tools • Environments • Tasks • Bootstrap

## What is mise? mise (pronounced "meez", short for _mise-en-place_) manages a project's dev tools, environment variables, and tasks from one `mise.toml` that works across your shell, editor, and CI: ```toml [tools] node = "24" python = "3.14" rust = "stable" "cargo:cargo-nextest" = "0.9" "github:BurntSushi/ripgrep" = "15" "npm:prettier" = "3" [env] NODE_ENV = "development" _.file = ".env" _.path = "./node_modules/.bin" [tasks.build] description = "Build the application" run = "npm run build" [tasks.test] description = "Run the test suite" depends = ["build"] run = "pytest && npm test" ``` - Install [dev tools](https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/) such as Node.js, Python, Go, Rust, and Terraform from a [registry of 1,000+ tools](https://mise.jdx.dev/registry.html) or directly from [backends](https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/backends/) like GitHub releases, Aqua, Cargo, npm, and PyPI, with separate versions per project. - Load [environment variables](https://mise.jdx.dev/environments/), `.env` files, `PATH` entries, virtualenvs, and [secrets](https://mise.jdx.dev/environments/secrets/) automatically as you enter a directory. - Run [tasks](https://mise.jdx.dev/tasks/) defined in `mise.toml` or as scripts in `mise-tasks/`, with dependencies, parallel execution, file watching, and the project's tools and environment already configured. - Set up a machine with [`mise bootstrap`](https://mise.jdx.dev/bootstrap.html) and [`mise dot apply`](https://mise.jdx.dev/dotfiles.html) to apply system packages, dotfiles, Git repositories, macOS defaults, and background services. Each part works without the others, so you can start with a single tool or task. A project that already has `.nvmrc`, `.python-version`, or another [idiomatic version file](https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/versions.html#idiomatic-version-files) can keep it: mise reads those files once you enable them. [![Demo of mise managing tools](./docs/tapes/demo.gif)](https://mise.jdx.dev/demo.html) See the [demo transcript](https://mise.jdx.dev/demo.html#transcript) for the commands shown above. ## Quickstart ### 1. Install mise On macOS or Linux: ```sh curl -fsSL https://mise.run | sh ~/.local/bin/mise --version ``` On Windows, run `irm https://mise.run/powershell | iex` in PowerShell, or `winget install jdx.mise`. For Homebrew, apt, dnf, Scoop, and other package managers, see [Installing mise](https://mise.jdx.dev/installing-mise.html). The installer places the binary at `~/.local/bin/mise`. If `~/.local/bin` is not on your `PATH` yet, run `~/.local/bin/mise` in place of `mise` until you activate mise in step 4. ### 2. Run a tool without changing your shell ```sh mise exec node@24 -- node --version # v24.x.x ``` [`mise exec`](https://mise.jdx.dev/cli/exec.html) downloads Node.js 24 if needed and runs the command after `--` with that version on `PATH`. Your shell and config files stay untouched. ### 3. Configure a project Create a project directory, select Node.js 24, set an environment variable, and add a task: ```sh mkdir my-project && cd my-project mise use node@24 mise set NODE_ENV=development mise tasks add hello -- node -e "console.log(process.version, process.env.NODE_ENV)" ``` These commands install Node.js 24 and write `mise.toml`: ```toml [tools] node = "24" [env] NODE_ENV = "development" [tasks.hello] run = "node -e 'console.log(process.version, process.env.NODE_ENV)'" ``` Run the task with [`mise run`](https://mise.jdx.dev/cli/run.html): ```sh mise run hello # [hello] $ node -e 'console.log(process.version, process.env.NODE_ENV)' # v24.x.x development ``` Commit `mise.toml` so teammates and CI get the same setup when they run `mise install` or `mise run`. `"24"` requests the latest release in the Node.js 24 series; run `mise lock` to record exact versions and checksums in a [lockfile](https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/mise-lock.html), or `mise use --global node@24` to set a personal default in `~/.config/mise/config.toml`. ### 4. Activate mise in your shell (optional) Shell activation updates `PATH` and project environment variables whenever you change directories, so you can invoke `node` directly without `mise exec`. If you installed with `mise.run`, run the command for your shell once, then open a new terminal: ```sh # bash echo 'eval "$(~/.local/bin/mise activate bash)"' >> ~/.bashrc # zsh echo 'eval "$(~/.local/bin/mise activate zsh)"' >> "${ZDOTDIR:-$HOME}/.zshrc" # fish mkdir -p ~/.config/fish echo '~/.local/bin/mise activate fish | source' >> ~/.config/fish/config.fish ``` If a package manager installed mise, use `mise` in place of `~/.local/bin/mise`. With Homebrew, fish activates mise without this step. For PowerShell, Nushell, Elvish, Xonsh, and IDE or CI shims, see [Shell setup](https://mise.jdx.dev/shell-setup.html) and [Shims](https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/shims.html). ## Everyday commands | Command | Action | | --------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- | | `mise use node@24` | Install a tool and record it in the current project's `mise.toml` | | `mise use --global node@24` | Install a tool and set it as your global default | | `mise install` | Install all tools declared in the active config files | | `mise exec -- ` | Run a command with the project's tools and environment | | `mise run ` | Run a project task with its dependencies, tools, and environment | | `mise set KEY=value` | Set an environment variable in `mise.toml` | | `mise env` | Print the resolved environment variables and `PATH` changes | | `mise ls --current` | List the tool versions active in the current directory | | `mise outdated` | List tools with newer releases than the installed version | | `mise upgrade` | Install those newer releases | | `mise lock` | Write exact tool versions and checksums to `mise.lock` | | `mise config ls` | Show the config files loaded for the current directory | | `mise doctor` | Check your mise installation, shell activation, and configuration | ## Set up a machine with mise bootstrap Beyond project directories, `~/.config/mise/config.toml` can declare the state of your machine: ```toml [bootstrap.packages] "apt:build-essential" = "latest" "brew:jq" = "latest" [bootstrap.repos] "~/src/app" = { url = "https://github.com/you/app.git" } [dotfiles] "~/.zshrc" = { mode = "track" } ``` Preview and apply the configuration, or bootstrap a new machine directly from a Git repository: ```sh mise bootstrap --dry-run mise bootstrap mise bootstrap --adopt you/dotfiles ``` See [Bootstrap](https://mise.jdx.dev/bootstrap.html) and [Dotfiles](https://mise.jdx.dev/dotfiles.html) for supported package managers, dotfile tracking and templating, services, and remote SSH targets. ## Documentation | Topic | Guides | | ----------------------------- | Report bugs in [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/jdx/mise/issues). Check [Troubleshooting](https://mise.jdx.dev/troubleshooting.html) first, and include the command you ran, a minimal `mise.toml`, the expected and actual behavior, and your `mise doctor` output after reviewing it for private details. - Ask questions and share ideas in [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions). - Chat with the community on [Discord](https://discord.gg/mABnUDvP57).
